## The question

\vspace{1.5em}

\begin{center}
\Large\bfseries\color{econblue}
What is an amount in one year's money\\[0.1em]
worth in another year's money?
\end{center}

\vspace{1em}

\begin{center}
\normalsize\itshape
Thirteen currencies, two inflation measures, one tidy interface.
\end{center}

::: notes
Open with the core user question, not the package. Historical price
adjustment is a routine operation across journalism, economic history,
accounting, and everyday writing. The R ecosystem has delivered it
piecemeal. 60 seconds.
:::


## Why it matters

- **Journalism**: what is that 1970 salary worth in today's money?
- **Economic history**: deflating nineteenth- and twentieth-century wages to a common unit
- **Accounting and compliance**: revaluing historical assets, legacy contracts, and long-dated liabilities
- **Public policy**: comparing government spending, wages, and benefits across decades

::: notes
Four distinct stakeholder groups, four live use cases. Journalism and
accounting dominate volume; economic history dominates depth. Flag
the 2021 to 2023 inflation spike as fresh demand for all four. 60 seconds.
:::



## What is already out there

- **`priceR`**: pricing-related toolkit with some inflation helpers, broader scope\footnote{\scriptsize Condamin (2022), \textit{priceR: Economics and Pricing Tools}, R package on CRAN.}
- **`quantmod`**: pulls CPI series from FRED but leaves adjustment to the user
- **`WDI`**: fetches World Bank series but does not adjust values directly
- **Bespoke spreadsheets**: ad hoc, single-currency, hard to audit

\vspace{0.5em}

The gap: **no purpose-built tool that bundles the canonical indices and exposes a symmetric pair of adjustment functions**.

::: notes
Respect existing packages. priceR is the closest neighbour but has a
different primary focus. quantmod and WDI are data pipes, not
adjusters. inflateR is the purpose-built tool. 45 seconds.
:::



## What inflateR offers

1. **Coverage**: thirteen currencies (GBP, USD, AUD, EUR, CAD, JPY, CNY, CHF, NZD, INR, KRW, BRL, NOK), 1960 to 2024
2. **Interface**: four adjustment functions in two symmetric pairs, one cumulative/annualised rate helper, one metadata helper
3. **Provenance**: zero runtime dependencies, no API key, no network access, World Bank WDI data bundled

\vspace{0.5em}

On CRAN since March 2026. CPI and GDP deflator both exposed\footnote{\scriptsize World Bank Development Indicators, series \texttt{FP.CPI.TOTL} and \texttt{NY.GDP.DEFL.ZS}, rescaled to 2020 = 100.}.

::: notes
Three bullets, three selling points. The zero-runtime-dependency claim
is the distinguishing feature: it means the package works in airgapped
environments, in CI pipelines, and in courses where students cannot
hit external APIs. 45 seconds.
:::

## Central formulas

\vspace{0.3em}

\textbf{Forward adjustment} (historical to present):
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{adjust\_inflation}(a,\ s \to t) = a \cdot \frac{I_t}{I_s}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Cumulative inflation rate} between years $s$ and $t$:
\begin{equation}
\pi_{s \to t} = \frac{I_t}{I_s} - 1
\end{equation}

\textbf{Annualised inflation rate} for $n = t - s$ years:
\begin{equation}
\pi_{\mathrm{ann}} = \left(\frac{I_t}{I_s}\right)^{1/n} - 1
\end{equation}

::: notes
Three equations. Do not read them aloud. Point at the simple ratio in
the forward adjustment and the geometric root in the annualised rate.
The reverse adjustment is the multiplicative inverse: that symmetry is
why the package exposes two explicit function pairs rather than one.
60 seconds.
:::



## Package at a glance

::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}

Function families:

- **CPI adjustment**: `adjust_inflation()`, `historical_value()`
- **GDP deflator adjustment**: `adjust_real()`, `historical_real()`
- **Rates**: `inflation_rate()` (cumulative or annualised)
- **Metadata**: `list_currencies()`

Deps: base R only. R $\geq$ 3.5.0. No API key, no network.

:::
::: {.column width="40%"}

\begin{block}{Direction-measure matrix}
Two directions (forward and reverse) times two measures (CPI and deflator) = four core functions.

Every function accepts ISO code or country name.
\end{block}

:::
:::

::: notes
Two columns. Left lists the function families. Right highlights the
two-by-two matrix in the blue block. Zero-dependency claim sits in the
deps line, understated but load-bearing. 45 seconds.
:::



## Minimal working example

```r
library(inflateR)

# Forward: 1990 GBP 30,000 salary in today's money
adjust_inflation(30000, from_year = 1990, currency = "GBP")

# Reverse: today's GBP 50,000 in 1990 equivalent
historical_value(50000, to_year = 1990, currency = "GBP")

# Rate: annualised CPI inflation for GBP, 1970 to 2024
inflation_rate("GBP", from_year = 1970, to_year = 2024,
               annualised = TRUE)
```

\footnotesize
Every function is vectorised over `amount`, so bulk conversion of a
column of historical prices requires no loop.

::: notes
Live-read the code. Three calls, three numeric returns, no
data-wrangling. That is the entire user experience. Point at the
symmetry between lines two and three: same pair, opposite direction.
60 seconds.
:::



## UK real median weekly earnings, 1980 to 2024

**Data.** ONS Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings (ASHE). Median gross weekly pay for full-time employees, 1980 to 2024 as published.

**Question.** *Have UK real wages stagnated since the 2010 peak?*

**Why this case.** Canonical UK applied-labour question over the past fifteen years\footnote{\scriptsize Blundell, Joyce, Keiller \& Ziliak (2023), \textit{The dynamics of real wages in the UK}, and Giupponi \& Machin (2023) on wage stagnation.}. Nominal series hides the phenomenon entirely; CPI deflation via a single function call reveals it. Reproducible with one line of `adjust_inflation()`.

::: notes
Setup only. No results on this slide. Point forward: the hero figure
is next. Name the data source, the period, the canonical question, and
the role of the package. The headline number comes on the next slide.
45 seconds.
:::


::: notes
The money slide. Ninety seconds. Walk the audience through each
series: nominal wages grew twelve per cent between 2010 and 2024, but
real wages fell by nearly six per cent. The nominal view hides the
stagnation entirely. The package flips between the two with a single
function call. Pause before moving on.
:::



## Purchasing power has collapsed for GBP, USD, and JPY

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[height=0.68\textheight]{figures/fig5_power.pdf}
\end{center}

\vspace{-0.5em}

{\footnotesize\itshape Purchasing power of 1 unit of currency relative to 1970, 1970 to 2024. GBP 7 per cent, USD 13 per cent, JPY 30 per cent. Computed via inverse \texttt{adjust\_inflation()}.}
```

::: notes
One operational example of the inverse call. Purchasing-power erosion
is a more intuitive framing for lay audiences than a multiplier.
Point at the GBP endpoint: seven per cent means GBP 1 in 1970 buys
what seven pence does today. JPY's flatter path is the Japan
deflation story. 60 seconds.
:::


## What inflateR does not yet do

- **World Bank WDI only**: native methodologies (ONS RPI, BLS chained CPI) differ modestly
- **No PPP conversion**: cross-country comparisons at a point in time need a separate step
- **Annual data only**: no monthly or quarterly adjustment out of the box
- **1960 start**: pre-1960 history requires users to supply an alternative series

\vspace{0.5em}

**v0.2.0 roadmap**: expanded currency coverage, optional PPP-adjusted cross-country conversion, higher-frequency data, and an `inflation_chart()` helper for plot output.

::: notes
Honest limitations. Name each one. The WDI choice is deliberate (it
buys cross-country comparability) but the trade-off is methodology
purity against a native calculator. Frame v0.2.0 as a commitment. 45
seconds.
:::
